email_section.preheader: The FDA's daily figure for most adults, and the factors that change yours.
email_section.body:
The FDA has cited 400 milligrams of caffeine a day for most adults, about two to three 12-fluid-ounce cups of coffee, as an amount not generally associated with negative effects. But "too much" varies with body weight, medications, medical conditions and sensitivity.

Three things worth checking this week:
- Your decaf: it typically has 2 to 15 milligrams in an 8-fluid-ounce cup.
- Your snacks and medicine cabinet: energy or protein bars, ice cream, chewing gum, supplements and over-the-counter medications can contain added caffeine.
- Your energy drink: generally 54 to 328 milligrams per 16 fluid ounces.

Signs you've had too much include a racing heart, jitters, trouble sleeping and an upset stomach. If you want to cut back, do it gradually.

Read the FDA's full caffeine guide

audience_versions.post:
Wondering how much caffeine a day is too much? The FDA's consumer guide gives a number, and a reason not to treat it as a hard line.

The number: for most adults, the FDA has cited 400 milligrams a day, about two to three 12-fluid-ounce cups of coffee, as an amount not generally associated with negative effects.

The reason: people vary widely in how sensitive they are to caffeine and how fast they eliminate it. Body weight, medications, certain medical conditions and individual sensitivity all change what "too much" means for you.

To count your own intake:
- Typical 12-fluid-ounce amounts: soft drinks 23 to 83 mg, green tea 37 mg, black tea 71 mg, brewed coffee 113 to 247 mg, energy drinks 41 to 246 mg.
- Add decaf (2 to 15 mg in an 8-fluid-ounce cup), bars, ice cream, gum, supplements and over-the-counter medications.
- Read the ingredient list: caffeine added on its own must be listed.

On the overdose question: the FDA estimates toxic effects like seizures can be seen with rapid consumption of around 1,200 milligrams, less than 1/2 teaspoon of pure caffeine. Signs of too much include increased heart rate, jitters, anxiety, insomnia and nausea.

Link to the full guide in the first comment.
audience_versions.what_changed: Opens on the daily-limit question these searchers type, explains why the number isn't a hard line, gives a way to count their own intake, and answers the overdose question the keywords show.

audience_versions.post:
Your customers are being told to ask you about caffeine.

The FDA's consumer guide says restaurants and other retail food establishments aren't required by law to tell customers how much caffeine is in what they serve, and it encourages customers to ask. Expect the question at the counter.

What the guide tells your customers:
- For most adults, the FDA has cited 400 milligrams a day, about two to three 12-fluid-ounce cups of coffee, as not generally associated with negative effects.
- Typical 12-fluid-ounce amounts: green tea 37 mg, black tea 71 mg, regular brewed coffee 113 to 247 mg, energy drinks 41 to 246 mg.
- Decaf isn't caffeine-free: typically 2 to 15 mg in an 8-fluid-ounce cup.
- "Too much" varies with body weight, medications, medical conditions and sensitivity, and people who are pregnant or breastfeeding are told to talk to a health care provider.

Two points for your menu and your staff:
- Medical experts advise against energy drinks for children and teens, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics.
- By law, food companies are responsible for making sure any use of caffeine in their products is safe.

Knowing the caffeine in each drink you serve gives your staff an answer ready when someone asks.

Link to the FDA's guide in the first comment.
audience_versions.what_changed: Opens on customers being told to ask the retailer, frames the facts as what customers will hear, and adds the two points that matter behind the counter: energy drinks and teens, and who is responsible for safe use.

clean_transcript.text: Welcome to episode 12 of the Example Booking podcast.

clean_transcript.speaker: Theo Marsh
clean_transcript.text: Today I'm talking to Rosa Delacourt, who owns Example Hair Studio, about no-shows and the policy that fixed them.

clean_transcript.speaker: Theo Marsh
clean_transcript.text: So, take me back a year, because I know a lot of people listening are where you were then.

clean_transcript.speaker: Theo Marsh
clean_transcript.text: Where were you?

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: A year ago our no-show rate was 14 percent.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: That's roughly one empty chair out of every seven appointments.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: We have six stylists, so on a busy Saturday that was two or three empty chairs.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: And the worst part was color appointments, because those block two or three hours of a stylist's day.

clean_transcript.speaker: Theo Marsh
clean_transcript.text: What did you try first?

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: We tried, calling every client the day before.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: It took my front desk about an hour every afternoon, and honestly it barely moved the number.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: Half the calls went to voicemail anyway.

clean_transcript.speaker: Theo Marsh
clean_transcript.text: So what changed?

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: We wrote a real no-show policy.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: We had one before, but it was a line on a sign by the till that nobody read.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: The new one has three parts.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: First, clients get a text reminder 48 hours before the appointment and another one 2 hours before.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: Second, they can cancel or move the booking from that text, up to 24 hours ahead, with no charge.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: And third, for color and anything over two hours, we take a deposit when they book.

clean_transcript.speaker: Theo Marsh
clean_transcript.text: What does the reminder actually say?

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: It's short.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: Their name, the stylist, the time, and one line that says the deposit is kept if they cancel inside 24 hours.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: Then a link to move or cancel.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: We tried a friendlier, longer version and fewer people tapped the link.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: Honestly, I was scared we'd lose people.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: We didn't, as far as I can tell.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: Two regulars complained in the first month, and both of them still book with us.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: I think the key was that we explained it in person before it ever showed up on a booking.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: Every stylist told their clients at checkout for about three weeks before we switched it on.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: So nobody met the deposit for the first time on a screen.

clean_transcript.speaker: Theo Marsh
clean_transcript.text: And the numbers?

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: After three months the no-show rate was 4 percent.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: So, from 14 down to 4.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: And the 24-hour window matters as much as the deposit, because a cancellation the day before is a slot we can still fill.

clean_transcript.speaker: Theo Marsh
clean_transcript.text: How do you fill it?

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: We keep a waitlist.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: When someone cancels, the first three people on the list get a text, and the first one to reply gets the slot.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: Last month we had 11 late cancellations and the waitlist filled 9 of them.

clean_transcript.speaker: Theo Marsh
clean_transcript.text: What happens when someone still doesn't show up?

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: The first time, we forgive it and we tell them we forgave it.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: The second time, we keep the deposit.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: We've only had to do that a handful of times, and it was always for a color appointment.

clean_transcript.speaker: Theo Marsh

clean_transcript.speaker: Theo Marsh
clean_transcript.text: They were spending an hour a day on calls.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: That's gone.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: Now it's maybe ten minutes in the morning, checking the waitlist replies.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt
clean_transcript.text: They spend that time on the clients who are actually in the building.

clean_transcript.speaker: Theo Marsh
clean_transcript.text: A lot of owners have told us they're nervous that clients will just go somewhere else.

clean_transcript.speaker: Rosa Delacourt

title.text: Salon No-Show Policy: How One Studio Got to 4%

meta_description.text: A salon no-show policy that took one hair studio from 14% to 4% no-shows in three months: two reminders, a 24-hour window, deposits and a waitlist.

intro.text: Rosa Delacourt owns Example Hair Studio, a salon with six stylists. On episode 12 of the Example Booking podcast she explained the salon no-show policy that took her no-show rate from 14 percent to 4 percent in three months.

paragraphs.text: A year earlier, 14 percent of appointments were no-shows, which Rosa puts at roughly one empty chair in every seven. Color appointments hurt most, because each one blocks two or three hours. Calling every client the day before took the front desk about an hour each afternoon and, she says, barely moved the number.

sections.h2: The salon no-show policy, in three parts

paragraphs.text: The new policy has three parts: a text reminder 48 hours before the appointment and another 2 hours before; cancelling or moving the booking from that text up to 24 hours ahead, with no charge; and a deposit taken at booking for color and anything over two hours.
The reminder is short: name, stylist, time, one line saying the deposit is kept for a cancellation inside 24 hours, and a link to move or cancel. A longer, friendlier version got fewer taps.

sections.h2: How salon clients took the no-show fee

paragraphs.text: Rosa expected to lose clients and, as far as she can tell, did not: two regulars complained in the first month, and both still book. She thinks the key was explaining the deposit in person first. Every stylist told clients about it at checkout for about three weeks before it was switched on.

When a client still doesn't show, the first time is forgiven, and the client is told so. The second time, the studio keeps the deposit, which Rosa says has happened only a handful of times, always for a color appointment.

quote.text: So nobody met the deposit for the first time on a screen.
quote.speaker: Rosa Delacourt

sections.h2: Filling late cancellations from a salon waitlist

paragraphs.text: After three months the no-show rate was 4 percent. Rosa says the 24-hour window matters as much as the deposit, because a cancellation the day before is a slot the studio can still fill. When someone cancels, the first three people on the waitlist get a text, and the first to reply gets the slot. Last month that filled 9 of 11 late cancellations.
The calls are gone too. Rosa says the front desk now spends maybe ten minutes in the morning on waitlist replies, and that time goes to the clients in the building.

sections.h2: Rosa's advice for a salon starting out

paragraphs.text: Start deposits with the appointments that hurt most when they're empty; for this studio that was color. Keep the fee out of the small print: say it out loud, and put it on the booking page and in the reminder text. Make cancelling easy.
She would keep the deposit for color, but thinks one for a quick trim would probably cost more goodwill than it saves.

quote.text: If moving a booking takes one tap, people move it instead of just not showing up.
quote.speaker: Rosa Delacourt

key_takeaways.text: Two text reminders, 48 hours and 2 hours before, each with a link to move or cancel.
A deposit only where an empty chair costs most, explained in person first, which Rosa thinks was the key.
A waitlist text to the first three people turns a cancellation into a booking.
